searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's, one left unspent. Six were restricted to a house's own domain (jermann.it, liviofelluga.it, schiopetto.it, gravner.it and radikon.it, one each, and jermann.it in the search on the harvest) and are read as primary through their summaries; the Rosazzo and Collio rules were read through AIS copies of the disciplinari. One search shared by Gravner and Radikon settled the serving temperature of the two orange wines on Decanter's advice; one on Radikon's own serving advice returned nothing usable. No WebFetch was tried. The commit of the fragment gave the split as Jermann 8, Felluga 4, Schiopetto 4, Gravner 6, Radikon 3 and shared 2; the true split is the one here, with the same total.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the facts that matter most: the dates and the people, the classifications, the sites and the making; a fact the Codex library states stood on the library unless a search contradicted it.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where the accounts disagreed the record now says so or says less; where a claim rested on one account only it was cut; where the author's primary source holds a fact the refuter could not reach again, it stands and is listed as open.

Sources whose address or title names a living writer or grower (a wine wiki under a first name, a merchant's producer page under the grower's name, a critic's blog address) were read in the results but never cited.

tested: Founded 1881 and the founder: Meininger, vino.com and clickwine have the house founded by Anton Jermann in 1881, who left Burgenland and then vineyards in Slovenia for Friuli: confirmed as the house's account; his dates not found, so he is described.

The maker of Tunina: the house's timeline has the son of the house trained at Conegliano and San Michele, back from a research sabbatical overseas: confirmed, worked abroad softened to studied abroad for a time; he is living and never named.
The first trials of the 1973 harvest and the first wine sold as Vintage Tunina of the 1975: the house's timeline and a house news page: confirmed, and the story question's key with it.

The name: the house and Xtrawine give a former owner of the land called Tunina and Casanova's Venetian housekeeper: confirmed as the house tells it; one merchant ties the name to a daughter of the family, left open.

The grapes: the house's factsheet lists Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Ribolla Gialla and Malvasia; the house's Picolit page says Picolit went into Vintage Tunina and Capo Martino for many years before a Picolit of its own from 2006: changed to for many years.
The harvest: the house has the grapes picked late, about two weeks after the usual harvest, at Ronco del Fortino, guyot and cappuccina trained: confirmed.

The making: Decanter has the grapes picked together, whole bunch pressed and fermented together, unwooded in the 1990s with discreet oak since and long on fine lees; a review of the 2022 has them fermented apart and blended, Saratoga Wine's sheet of the 2023 steel to about six per cent alcohol and part finished in large Slavonian oak, a house page of 2017 cement vats: changed to the accounts differing, whole bunch pressing cut.
The site: one account places Ronco del Fortino in the heart of the Collio on marl and sandstone of Eocene origin, another near Gorizia; none read placed it in Villanova di Farra: changed.
The majority of 2021 passing to Marchesi Antinori: Meininger and the author's Decanter and Gambero Rosso: confirmed.
Vinnae: Superiore.de and Callmewine give Ribolla Gialla with a little Friulano and Riesling Renano: changed from a Ribolla alone.

The rules of the house: the guide's wine of the year for the 1997 is a rating and is cut; nobody living named; no price or volatile figure (the house's hectares met and kept out); British spelling; no dash.

tested: Livio Felluga's dates and place of birth: the Messaggero Veneto by way of Dissapore and Blitz Quotidiano give Isola d'Istria in 1914 (one gives 1 September) and death at his home in Brazzano a few days before Christmas at 102; producer profiles give 2016: confirmed.

His coming to Friuli: profiles place him at the foot of the Rosazzo hills at the end of the 1930s, his plans cut short by the call to the front, and the vineyards near Rosazzo bought after the war: changed from the 1930s and the 1950s.
Founded 1956: profiles have the house founded by him at Brazzano in 1956, as the library gives it: confirmed.

The map label: the house's own site has the label of the geographical map conceived by him in 1956; the obituaries have it adopted when there were no DOCs yet, to show where the wine came from: confirmed and dated by the house's account.

Terre Alte: the house's site has it launched in 1981, the must settled and fermented in steel, moved to oak barrels to finish its alcoholic and malolactic fermentations, kept on its lees and bottled in summer: confirmed.

Rosazzo: the AIS copy of the disciplinare gives at least half Friulano, Sauvignon and Pinot Bianco or Chardonnay a fifth to three tenths each and Ribolla Gialla no more than a tenth, approved by the decree of 14 October 2011; Gambero Rosso has Rosazzo a subzone of the Colli Orientali until 2011: confirmed, the subzone added.
The Cappuccina training of the vines: not found for Felluga in any search (the house's Tunina sheet gives guyot and cappuccina for Jermann): cut.
The rules of the house: the four children named in a profile are living and kept out; no price or volatile figure (export markets met and kept out); British spelling; no dash.

tested: Mario Schiopetto's dates: Vinous gives 1930 and death in 2003 at seventy two; Decanter's obituary of April 2003 has him dead at seventy two; one merchant gives 2002: confirmed as 1930 to 2003.

The inn and the travels: Vinous and Grandi Bottiglie have the family's osteria in Udine, a youth as a fireman, travels to cellars across Europe, French finesse and above all German white winemaking: confirmed.
The first Tocai of 1965: the house's Friulano sheet gives first production 1965; Superiore and Vinous the same: confirmed.

The steel and the cold: Grandi Bottiglie and Superiore credit him with bringing cold fermentation and selected yeasts to Friuli and keeping wine in steel: confirmed as among the first in Friuli; the library's Italy is not.

The lease and the purchase: Superiore has vines rented from the Archbishop of Gorizia at Spessa di Capriva from 1965 and bought in 1989; the house's history begins with the lease in 1970: changed to the house's account with the other year told.
The making of the Friulano: the house's sheet of the 2019 gives 16 degrees Celsius, ten to twelve days in steel, eight months in steel on the lees and at least five months in bottle: confirmed.
The Collio DOC of 1968: the disciplinare gives the decree of 24 May 1968: confirmed. The name Tocai off EU labels after 31 March 2007: confirmed.
Pinot Bianco first produced in 1967: the house's sheet: confirmed. Blanc des Rosis: the house's page has a Friulano led blend raised eight months on the lees in steel: changed from a field blend.
The sale of 2014: Superiore and Callmewine have the estate pass to a family in 2014: confirmed; the family is living and not named.
The rules of the house: the library's benchmark is not used; nobody living named; British spelling; no dash.

tested: The house of 1901: Primal Wine and a merchant have the family buy a house and land at Oslavia in 1901: confirmed; founded stays empty, as the library has it.

The steel and barriques of the 1980s: Decanter's profile has steel tanks replacing the old casks and French barriques installed; another account has the steel sold in 1997: kept, on Decanter, and open.

The hail of 1996: Decanter's profile has hail destroying ninety five per cent of the Ribolla crop and an experimental treatment of what was left, the first skin macerated Ribolla released from the 1997: changed from a small part left.

Georgia and the amphorae: Decanter has the journey of 2000 and the first amphora imported in 2001, the whole cellar in amphora by 2005; Superiore dates the amphora method to 2001: changed from the whites in clay from then on.

The vines pulled up: one account has the last Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Riesling Italico of 2012 and the international varieties phased out after it, a merchant quoting the estate the last Breg of 2011; Ribolla and Pignolo remain: changed to early in the 2010s.

Bianco Breg: Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Pinot Grigio and Riesling Italico by two merchants: named. Rosso Gravner: the house's sheet for the 2010 is titled Merlot with a small part of another grape, with more than four weeks of maceration in buried Georgian amphorae and four years in Slavonian oak: confirmed against the library's Pignolo.

The making of the Ribolla: Different Drop, Callmewine and others give about six months on the skins in amphora, a further six months or at least five without them, six years in large oak and release some seven years after harvest; the International Wine Challenge reports glass tanks ordered in 2024 to take part of the oak time: kept, hedged as a rule.
No temperature control: not found in any search: cut.

The serving temperature: Decanter advises serving Gravner and Radikon close to room temperature, tasting first at 12 to 14 degrees Celsius and warming if closed; merchants give 14 to 16 and 16 to 18: changed from 12 to 14.
The rules of the house: the grower is living and never named; a merchant's page whose address names him was not cited; British spelling; no dash.

tested: The first bottling: the house's history lists, under 1980, the first bottling of the 1979 vintage, five wines among them Ribolla Gialla and Tocai: confirmed, the first wine made plural.
Oslavje of 1992: the house's history gives a blend of Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon and Chardonnay: confirmed; Verve and Flatiron list later bottlings as Chardonnay and Sauvignon: the hedge stands.

The turning point of 1995, Oslavje macerated for eight days from 1997, half the wine without sulphur in 2001, every wine three months on its skins with no sulphites, a new cork and new bottle sizes in 2002: the house's history: confirmed, the new cork added.

The grandfather: importers name Franz Mikulus as the man who planted Ribolla on the hill: confirmed and described, his dates not found; one account calls the maceration of 1995 a return to his way: cut as one source.
The death: the house's memorial and the author's Decanter give 11 September 2016, a critic's piece at sixty two: confirmed; the birth year is not in two sources, so he is described.

The making: an importer gives oak vats for two to four months on the skins and three years in casks of 25 to 35 hectolitres, another large Slavonian oak, a merchant forty eight months in foudres; the house's timeline three months for every wine since 2002: changed to about three months and three years or more; open vats, no temperature control and unfiltered not found: cut.
The serving temperature: Decanter's advice for Radikon and Gravner: changed from 12 to 14 to 14 to 16; the house's own advice was not found.
The bottles: half litre and litre listings at Flatiron for Oslavje: confirmed for Oslavje; the trap no longer speaks for every wine of the house.
The rules of the house: the son is living and never named; a critic's address that names him was not cited; British spelling; no dash.
